S1: Four artifacts, one system. (a) Each artifact is drawn with its own form. Learn is an ordered staircase of lesson tiles, Atlas a registry of record cells with one cell selected, Labs a console with a run control, and Report a ruled page carrying a figure. The four shapes recur wherever the four artifacts recur, and the four colours are what survive when the colour does not. (b) A rail under the four carries the shared resource identifier. One correction sits on the rail, and the dashed branches carry it to the identifier chip of each artifact, which is the route a correction takes. The figure shows the coupling and nothing more. It carries no counts, no coverage claim and no measured outcome.
S2: Four classes of statement. The editorial guide makes each statement's authority visible, and the four classes differ in kind rather than in degree, so each is drawn instead of being placed on a scale. (a) An observed source fact shows the opened document and the link that ties it to a claim. (b) A project decision shows several inputs meeting at one node. (c) An open question shows an object that is not yet defined, ringed and spoked. (d) Future work shows tiles that are planned and not yet built. Solid borders mark the two classes that assert something and dashed borders the two that do not, which is the only grouping the guide supports.
S3: Target to candidate. A stage table of nine stages becomes a pipeline that states what a funnel normally hides. Each cell carries the stage, the decision in question form, a narrowing drawn as a taper with candidates in it, and the branch that leaves the taper to the failure mode the table records for that stage. The route between the two rows gives the order. The dots in a taper are a drawing convention, and the figure reports no count, rate or probability. It also omits the strong cheap baseline that the same table records for every stage.
S4: Stage evidence. The same nine stages, each drawn as a form whose fields are the records that stage cannot be argued without, in the wording of the stage table. The filled square at the head of a field marks it as required. The contracts differ from stage to stage, and a stage that borrows another stage's contract has quietly changed what the stage means. The figure shows the evidence contract only. It does not show the strong cheap baseline or the failure modes, which the decision pipeline carries.
S5: Prerequisite graph over the six learning paths. Ten distinct lessons are named as a prerequisite somewhere in the catalogue, and twenty-one prerequisite relations connect them to the five specialist routes. A lesson's badge gives the number of routes that require it, so the hub is visible without reading the edges, and a route's badge gives the number of lessons the route lists. A solid edge is a prerequisite the catalogue states. A dashed edge is a lesson the core route also lists, which is a different relation and is drawn as a different relation. The core route names no prerequisite of its own. The badges are counts from the catalogue, not difficulty, depth or coverage.
S6: Seven-dimensional openness. (a) and (b) are two catalogue records drawn as the forms they are, a model and a dataset, and they are close to opposites. Where the model has inference code and weights, the dataset has nothing to open there, and the dataset's one available dimension is the data recipe. (c) is the vocabulary of the four states, available, not available, not applicable and unverified, where unverified records that no claim is made. (d) is the two axes the schema holds separate from openness, lifecycle status and access level. The two records are a dated snapshot from the catalogue review of 21 October 2026, and a later re-review can change their states.
S7: Frozen evaluation. The protocol is frozen before the held-out test result is looked at, and the test set is opened once. The sequence runs from the written protocol through the freeze, the structural and finite-output pretests on training and validation data, the single opening, to the reviewed summary. A bug found after the test has been opened is reported as a protocol-invalidating error, and the barred loop is the prohibition on a second opening. The figure carries no measured value, and the two pretests are drawn as they pass rather than as they can fail.
